passage: In a dorm room in Warsaw, Emil and Wei opened the order log again. Their delivery service for student errands had been slow all autumn: a parcel here, a shopping run there. But tonight, sorting by date, Wei pointed. "Look at these bunches. December, January, June. Nearly everything is print jobs, and always the week before exams." Emil scrolled. "Lecture notes. People print them and hate queueing." They stopped the errands. For two days they wrote a plan: upload notes, choose a pickup time, collect from a locker outside the library. In the next exam period, orders tripled. Wei laughed at the counter. "We did not lose the idea. We just found the part people wanted."

qa.q: In which months did Wei notice bunches of print jobs?
qa.a: Wei noticed bunches of print jobs in December, January and June.

qa.q: What is Wei feeling when pointing at the bunches in the log?
qa.a: Wei feels a spark of excitement and discovery, pointing quickly as a pattern shows up in the data.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the founders use to check the new focus, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a few students what they would pay for printing and pickup, because the log shows what happened but not what students would keep using.

qa.q: How might a student with exams next week see the new service?
qa.a: A student uploads notes, picks a pickup time and collects them from a locker, so the student avoids the queue during a stressful week.

grounding: Shows adaptive replanning: noticing what customers actually used and narrowing the service to notes and printing, after which orders grew.

passage: In the campus incubator's small meeting room, Sabina spread three months of order sheets across the table. Their service had started as "anything delivered to your hostel room": snacks, stationery, medicines, printouts. Pema, her cofounder, had highlighted every printout order in yellow. The pages were mostly yellow in two places: the weeks before mid-terms and the weeks before finals. "Snacks, fourteen orders in three months," Pema said. "Printouts, two hundred and six." Sabina tapped the yellow. "People don't need us to deliver everything. They need notes printed at midnight before an exam." Their mentor, listening from the corner, raised an eyebrow. "So what changes?" Sabina took a breath. "We drop snacks and medicines. We become notes and printing only, and we stay open till 2 am in exam weeks." The next exam season, orders tripled.

qa.q: How many printout orders were there in three months?
How did Sabina feel on seeing the yellow pages?
qa.a: Sabina felt a spark of realisation and excitement, seeing that printouts were what people truly needed.

qa.q: What else could they add to the narrowed service?
qa.a: They could offer binding or a pickup point near the library, and keep checking the data each exam season.

qa.q: How might students see the change?
qa.a: Students get a reliable way to print notes late before exams, which is exactly the need they were already showing.

grounding: Shows founders noticing customers mostly use the service for exam-week printouts, narrowing it to notes and printing, and seeing orders grow.

passage:
Subject: I think we should change what we are
Zubin,
I went through all 312 orders from August to November last night. Here's what I found.
We started as a general errand service for the hostels. But 71% of our orders were printouts, and almost all of them came in the ten days before exams. Grocery runs: 18 orders. Courier pickups: 9. The rest barely exist.
So the customers have already told us what we are. We just haven't listened.
My proposal: from December, we stop general errands and only print and deliver notes. We tie up with the print shop by the gate, take orders on a simple form, and deliver to rooms twice a night during exam weeks.
I know you liked the do-everything idea. So did I. But the numbers aren't close.
Can we talk tomorrow after the lab?
Suraj

qa.q: How many grocery runs were there?
How does Suraj feel about proposing the change?
qa.a: Suraj feels sure because of the numbers, but a little uneasy, knowing Zubin liked the do-everything idea.

qa.q: What else could they do in the first exam season after the change?
qa.a: They could track orders and delivery times closely and ask users what else would help, so they keep adjusting.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel reading the email?
qa.a: Zubin may feel a pang at letting go of the do-everything idea, but the clear numbers make it hard to disagree.

grounding: Illustrates a founder spotting that most orders are exam-week printouts and proposing to narrow the service to notes and printing.
